evidence: src/domain/errors/DomainErrors.ts: abstract DomainError with ValidationError, NotFoundError and ConflictError all extending it. This is one consistent error hierarchy.
src/domain/errors/DomainErrors.ts: NotFoundError(entity, id) is the only place that formats the message "${entity} '${id}' was not found".
src/domain/services/TaskAssignmentService.ts: assign() throws new NotFoundError('User', userId), so it uses the module's error abstraction instead of a raw Error.

src/domain/services/TaskAssignmentService.ts: it looks up users through the UserRepository port (this.users.findById) and changes the task through the entity method task.assignTo(user.id), so the abstractions are not bypassed.
src/domain/services/TaskAssignmentService.ts: the doc comment states one invariant ('only existing users can be assigned'), and that invariant is enforced only in assign().
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files belong to the domain concern of the task-management model. DomainErrors.ts defines one error hierarchy rooted at the abstract DomainError. TaskAssignmentService.ts holds a single domain invariant: only users who exist can be assigned to a task. It enforces that invariant through the module's own abstractions. It looks up users through the UserRepository port, signals a missing user with the module's NotFoundError, and lets the entity change its own state through task.assignTo. It does not throw a raw Error or set fields on the task directly. Neither file duplicates a rule: the 'not found' message format is defined only in the NotFoundError constructor, and the assignment-existence check appears only in TaskAssignmentService.assign. Errors and services are different kinds of artifact, but both are parts of the same domain model, and the service uses the error hierarchy, so the unit is not split into unrelated concerns.
